title: POC Scoping: EU Dedicated + Data Residency / Region Pinning
next_steps: Redwood to send EU Dedicated sizing recommendation (GPU type/count) based on HelioBank traffic shape and context length distribution.
HelioBank to confirm target model(s), max context, and expected peak concurrency for the POC workloads.
Redwood to share beta plan + semantics for pinned_region/allowed_regions and the behavior on capacity exhaustion (no cross-region fallback by default).
Schedule technical deep dive on network path / IP allowlist / private connectivity options for EU Dedicated.
Redwood to provide sample audit event payloads for residency decisions/violations and confirm SIEM export path.
body:
Fireflies.ai Meeting Transcript

Title: POC Scoping: EU Dedicated + Data Residency / Region Pinning
Date: 2025-02-12
Start time: 10:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes

Attendees
- Lukas Meyer (Redwood Inference, AE)
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference, Solutions Engineering)
- Lauren Bishop (Redwood Inference, Dedicated Product)
- Naomi Feldman (Redwood Inference, Security & Compliance PM)
- Sven Adler (HelioBank, Head of Platform Engineering)
- Marianne Dupont (HelioBank, Security & Risk)
- Aditi Rao (HelioBank, ML Platform Lead)
- Jonas Richter (HelioBank, SRE)

Summary (auto-generated)
- HelioBank wants EU-only processing for LLM workloads and is evaluating Redwood Dedicated in an EU region for predictable throughput + isolation.
- Key requirement: deterministic region pinning (no implicit cross-region failover) with auditable allow/deny events.
- POC success criteria discussed: throughput targets, latency targets (TTFT + p95), and operational behaviors during capacity events.
- Redwood previewed beta timeline for hosted data residency enforcement and how the same policy model applies to Dedicated.

Topics
1) Workload overview (chat + embeddings, context sizes)
2) Dedicated in EU region: capacity sizing + isolation boundaries
3) Region pinning semantics: pinned_region vs allowed_regions, SDK/base URL pitfalls
4) Failure modes: capacity exhaustion, retries, routing fallback behavior
5) Audit logs and evidence: residency.violation + policy evaluated events
6) POC plan, timeline, and owners

Action items
- Lukas (Redwood): Send POC plan email w/ proposed timeline + owners by 2025-02-13
- Markus (Redwood): Share throughput sizing worksheet + recommended cluster config by 2025-02-14
- Naomi (Redwood): Share draft error code guidance + audit event examples by 2025-02-14
- Sven (HelioBank): Provide last-30-day traffic summary (peak RPS, prompt tokens, completion tokens, max context) by 2025-02-18
- Jonas (HelioBank): Confirm IP ranges + allowlist process for EU endpoints by 2025-02-18

Questions captured
- If EU is pinned and the EU capacity is exhausted, do you ever route to US automatically? (HelioBank: “we need no by default.”)
- Can we allow a temporary exception for cross-region processing during incidents? What approvals and how is it audited?
- What exactly is “in-scope data” for residency (prompts, completions, embeddings payload, logs, traces, analytics)?
- What’s the expected latency delta between Hosted EU and Dedicated EU, and what levers do we have for throughput?


Transcript

[00:00] Lukas Meyer: Alright, cool. Folks are joining. Um, thanks everyone. This is Lukas from Redwood. Goal today is POC scoping: EU Dedicated plus the data residency and the new region pinning behavior. We’ll keep it practical—what you need, what we can commit to, and next steps.

[00:24] Sven Adler: Sounds good.

[00:25] Marianne Dupont: Yes, thank you.

[00:27] Lukas Meyer: Quick intros maybe? Markus is our solutions engineer, Lauren runs Dedicated product, Naomi is security and compliance PM—she’s driving the residency enforcement work.

[00:40] Markus Klein: Hey everyone.

[00:41] Lauren Bishop: Hi.

[00:42] Naomi Feldman: Hi, thanks for having me.

[00:45] Sven Adler: I’m Sven, platform engineering. Aditi is ML platform, Jonas SRE, Marianne security and risk.

[00:53] Aditi Rao: Hi.

[00:54] Jonas Richter: Hey.

[00:56] Lukas Meyer: Great. Sven, do you want to start with the “why now” and what the POC is trying to prove?

[01:03] Sven Adler: Sure. We have internal chatbot, customer support assist, and some doc classification. We have EU customers, obviously, and the constraint from risk is EU-only processing. We’ve been prototyping with Azure OpenAI in West Europe, but cost is… not great, and control is limited. We looked at Bedrock too. We want something that we can pin to EU and not have weird failover to US, and we want a dedicated pool so other tenants don’t spike us.

[01:35] Marianne Dupont: And we need evidence. Like, if someone asks “prove nothing left the EU,” we need logs, audit trails, and clear contractual language.

[01:45] Naomi Feldman: Yep, makes sense.

[01:47] Lukas Meyer: Perfect. Markus, do you want to ask workload shape? That’ll drive sizing.

[01:52] Markus Klein: Yeah. Aditi, can you share roughly: concurrency, average prompt size, completion size, and max context? Even ballpark is fine.

[02:03] Aditi Rao: Ballpark. For chat: average prompt 1 to 2k tokens, completions 300 to 800, but sometimes 2k. Context window, we’re experimenting with 16k, maybe 32k later. Peak concurrency today is like 30 to 50 concurrent sessions during business hours. But we’re planning to integrate into a couple more apps, so it can double.

[02:29] Markus Klein: Great. And embeddings? Same platform?

[02:32] Aditi Rao: Embeddings is more batchy. We do like 100 docs at a time, each 1k tokens. Not constant.

[02:38] Jonas Richter: Peak request rate for chat is not insane, maybe 20 req/sec at peak? But we also care about tail latency because users wait.

[02:48] Markus Klein: Cool, that’s helpful.

[02:51] Lauren Bishop: On Dedicated, we can size to hit throughput and latency. Typically we talk about tokens/sec per GPU and headroom for spikes. We can do EU region—our current dedicated EU footprint is in “eu-west” (Ireland) for most customers, and we have “eu-central” capacity for some, depending on timeline.

[03:11] Sven Adler: For us, Ireland is okay. Main thing is EU boundary, not a specific country.

[03:17] Naomi Feldman: Right, and the enforcement policy is aligned to region boundary at the cloud region level. We’re not talking “EU legal” boundary in an abstract sense; it’s about the configured cloud region(s) where requests can be admitted and any side-effect writes can occur.

[03:33] Marianne Dupont: When you say “side-effect writes,” what’s included?

[03:36] Naomi Feldman: For the program we’re rolling out: prompts and completions payloads (if you enable any storage/persistence features), embeddings payloads, request metadata, logs and traces associated with the request path, and analytics/metering artifacts. We treat those as “in scope” for residency enforcement.

[03:57] Marianne Dupont: Okay, that matches our questionnaire.

[04:00] Lukas Meyer: The other key piece you called out is deterministic routing. Naomi, can you explain “pinned region” behavior in plain language?

[04:08] Naomi Feldman: Sure. The configuration model has two main concepts: a pinned_region and optionally allowed_regions. If pinned_region is set to, say, eu-west, then requests are admitted only if they’re going to be handled in eu-west. No cross-region fallback happens automatically. If a request comes in targeting us-east, or a client hits a US base URL, we return a clear error code—region mismatch—and we emit an audit event.

[04:36] Sven Adler: And on Dedicated specifically? Because dedicated implies there’s a cluster in EU anyway.

[04:40] Lauren Bishop: Correct. Dedicated is simpler: your capacity is physically in that EU region. The routing layer still exists—like which model shard, which node, etc.—but we don’t spill you to another region for capacity unless you explicitly set up multi-region dedicated, which you’re not.

[04:59] Jonas Richter: So the “no cross-region fallback” is default.

[05:02] Lauren Bishop: Yes for Dedicated. For Hosted, there used to be some fallback behavior in rare cases (capacity constraints) depending on product tier. The new enforcement changes make that deterministic when pinning is enabled. But for Dedicated, we already treat it as pinned unless you add another region.

[05:22] Markus Klein: The area where customers still get tripped up is the client hitting the wrong endpoint—like they have pinned EU but their SDK is still pointed at the default US hostname. Then it fails at admission. That’s actually good because it’s explicit.

[05:37] Aditi Rao: That’s exactly what happened in a different project. We had “region” set in config but DNS still went to the default.

[05:44] Markus Klein: Yep.

[05:45] Sven Adler: So what does the error look like? We need something actionable, not just 403.

[05:51] Naomi Feldman: It’ll be an HTTP error with a machine-readable code. Example would be something like RESIDENCY_REGION_MISMATCH. And the message includes: the request_region, the pinned_region, and remediation like “use the eu-west endpoint or set client region to eu-west.” Also we add a docs link.

[06:16] Marianne Dupont: And that’s logged in an audit trail?

[06:19] Naomi Feldman: Yes. There’s an event for policy evaluated (allow) and for violation (deny). You can export those to your SIEM. That’s part of the evidence story.

[06:31] Jonas Richter: If it’s allow events too, won’t that be super noisy?

[06:35] Naomi Feldman: Good question. We support sampling and filtering for “allow” in the export pipeline depending on plan and your needs. Violations are always emitted. Most compliance teams want at least aggregated allow evidence plus full violation detail.

[06:53] Sven Adler: For the POC, we probably want full fidelity for a short window, to validate.

[06:58] Naomi Feldman: Yep.

[07:00] Lukas Meyer: Let’s talk throughput targets. Jonas, you mentioned 20 req/sec peak. What’s your p95 latency target and time-to-first-token expectation?

[07:10] Jonas Richter: For chat, we want TTFT under 800ms ideally, p95 end-to-end under, I don’t know, 6 seconds for typical completions. But it depends on completion length. We stream tokens to UI.

[07:26] Markus Klein: Totally. We usually separate: TTFT and tokens/sec once streaming starts. For dedicated we can tune batching, but there’s a tradeoff with TTFT.

[07:36] Aditi Rao: We care about consistent experience more than absolute cheapest. But cost is still important.

[07:43] Lauren Bishop: That’s the dedicated sweet spot: predictable performance, and your unit economics become stable because you’re not sharing.

[07:51] Markus Klein: For sizing: if you’re doing 16k contexts sometimes, that drives GPU memory and KV cache. If you want, say, Llama 3.1 70B class models, then EU dedicated with H100s or equivalent is typical. But if you’re fine with smaller models, we can do Llama 8B/13B class with lower cost.

[08:12] Sven Adler: We’re leaning 70B for quality. But we can also test a smaller variant for some tasks.

[08:19] Markus Klein: Great. For POC we can do one primary model pinned, and optionally a secondary model but still in-region.

[08:26] Marianne Dupont: But no “fallback to US bigger model,” correct.

[08:29] Markus Klein: Correct.

[08:30] Naomi Feldman: Correct.

[08:32] Lukas Meyer: Lauren, what’s a typical starting dedicated configuration for that workload?

[08:37] Lauren Bishop: If it’s 70B with 16k and 20 req/sec peak, I’d start with something like 4 GPUs minimum, maybe 8 depending on concurrency and desired TTFT. But Markus should confirm with a sizing sheet based on token mix.

[08:54] Jonas Richter: If we double concurrency, will it queue or degrade latency?

[08:58] Markus Klein: It’ll queue if you exceed capacity. We can set concurrency limits and return 429s with retry-after rather than letting p95 explode. In dedicated we can also auto-scale within agreed bounds, but that’s a contract + infra question.

[09:15] Sven Adler: We’d rather have predictable than surprise cross-region.

[09:18] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[09:20] Marianne Dupont: On the “capacity exhaustion” topic—what happens if there’s an incident in eu-west? Like AWS issue.

[09:28] Lukas Meyer: This is the tough part. We can do multi-region active/standby, but that means you’re intentionally configuring allowed_regions to include another region. If policy is pinned EU-only, you can pick a second EU region, not US.

[09:43] Marianne Dupont: That’s acceptable—another EU region is okay. But not US.

[09:47] Naomi Feldman: The exception workflow exists if someone wants to temporarily allow cross-region beyond policy, but it’s an explicit process, approvals, expiry, and audit. For a bank, we generally recommend not using that except in extreme scenarios.

[10:04] Jonas Richter: So we could configure allowed_regions = [eu-west, eu-central] and pinned maybe… how does pinned work then?

[10:11] Naomi Feldman: Pinned means “must be this region.” Allowed means “may be any of these.” Typically you choose one. In a multi-region EU design you’d likely use allowed_regions and not pinned_region, or you’d pin at workspace level per environment (prod pinned eu-west, dr pinned eu-central) and fail over by switching pinned target via change control.

[10:34] Sven Adler: That’s closer to our operational model. We don’t want automatic.

[10:38] Naomi Feldman: Yep.

[10:40] Markus Klein: For POC, simplest is pinned_region=eu-west. Later we can discuss a DR region.

[10:47] Aditi Rao: On dedicated: are we sharing GPUs with other customers at all?

[10:51] Lauren Bishop: Dedicated means reserved capacity, isolated at the node pool level. You’re not sharing those GPUs for inference. Control plane is still managed, but the data plane is logically isolated. We can talk through network isolation too.

[11:09] Jonas Richter: Network wise, we need IP allowlisting at minimum. Private connectivity is a longer term maybe.

[11:15] Markus Klein: We can do static egress IPs from your side into our EU endpoint, and we can do allowlisting on our end for your source IPs. If you want private connectivity like PrivateLink, that’s possible but depends on region and lead time.

[11:34] Sven Adler: Let’s keep POC to IP allowlist.

[11:38] Lukas Meyer: Cool.

[11:39] Marianne Dupont: I want to go back to “logs and traces.” Are prompts stored in logs?

[11:45] Naomi Feldman: By default we do not dump full prompts into standard application logs. We have structured request metadata logs, and you can enable enhanced debugging/tracing that may capture more. For residency enforcement, regardless, any artifact that is stored is stored in-region when pinning is enabled. Also, we can configure redaction policies.

[12:08] Marianne Dupont: Okay. We’ll need that in writing.

[12:11] Lukas Meyer: We’ll follow up with the security pack.

[12:15] Markus Klein: Another practical point: In the SDK, we support specifying region hints. But we still recommend using the region-specific base URL for zero ambiguity.

[12:26] Aditi Rao: We’re in Python mostly.

[12:28] Markus Klein: Great. We can share examples: client = Redwood(region="eu-west") or base_url="https://eu-west.api.redwood.example"—whatever your tenant domain is. (I’m paraphrasing, Lukas will send the exact strings.)

[12:47] Jonas Richter: If someone misconfigures and hits US endpoint, it fails before compute, yes?

[12:52] Naomi Feldman: Correct. Admission check happens before model execution. That’s important for evidence: no processing in wrong region.

[13:02] Sven Adler: Good.

[13:04] Lukas Meyer: Let’s define success criteria for the POC. Sven/Aditi/Jonas, what do you want to measure to say “yes, we proceed”?

[13:13] Sven Adler: For me: residency enforcement is real—i.e., we can’t accidentally process in US, and we can prove it. Second: performance is stable during business hours, not spiky. Third: we can operate it—alerts, dashboards, basic runbook.

[13:33] Jonas Richter: Metrics wise, I want p95 TTFT and p95 total. Also error rates and rate limiting behavior. And I want to see what happens when we push over capacity—does it degrade gracefully.

[13:47] Aditi Rao: And quality—we need to compare model outputs between what we have today and Redwood’s model catalog. But that’s on us to run an eval set.

[13:57] Markus Klein: Perfect. Redwood can help with a prompt set harness if needed, but yes.

[14:03] Lauren Bishop: For dedicated, we’ll also monitor tokens/sec and GPU utilization to validate the sizing. If you see consistently >70% utilization at peak, we’ll recommend scale.

[14:16] Sven Adler: That’s fine.

[14:18] Marianne Dupont: Also, the exception process: I want to understand it even if we don’t use it.

[14:23] Naomi Feldman: Sure. The idea is: exceptions are time-bound, require approvals (security + GRC), and are recorded as audit entries with reason, scope, and expiry. Technically, it’s implemented as a policy override flag—like allow_cross_region_fallback—guarded and audited. But again, for POC we can leave it off.

[14:49] Marianne Dupont: Good.

[14:51] Lukas Meyer: Timeline: when do you want to start?

[14:54] Sven Adler: Ideally in two weeks. We have internal review next Friday. We can start integration right after.

[15:02] Lukas Meyer: That works. Dedicated provisioning lead time is usually 1–2 weeks for EU depending on GPU availability. Lauren, is that still accurate?

[15:11] Lauren Bishop: For eu-west, yes. If it’s H100 specifically, sometimes it’s tight but for a POC-sized pool we can usually do it.

[15:20] Markus Klein: We can start with a smaller pool for functional testing and scale up for load test.

[15:26] Jonas Richter: We can generate load from our staging env. We’ll need a window.

[15:31] Markus Klein: Perfect.

[15:33] Naomi Feldman: On beta for region pinning: the controls are in beta right now for a few customers. For Dedicated, it’s mostly about the audit events and the consistency of enforcement across logs/traces. We can enable the enforcement flag for your org during POC.

[15:52] Marianne Dupont: Beta means not GA, so what’s the support stance?

[15:56] Lukas Meyer: We treat it as guided POC with named owners, and we’ll give you a clear GA target date and what’s in-scope. We won’t claim “GA enterprise guarantee” until it’s GA, but the underlying behavior is there.

[16:10] Marianne Dupont: Understood.

[16:12] Sven Adler: Is there any scenario where data leaves EU even if compute is EU? Like analytics pipeline.

[16:19] Naomi Feldman: That’s specifically part of the enforcement project: downstream writes also respect residency. For example, if metering events are shipped, they’re shipped to an in-region sink. If a sink is misconfigured, the write is blocked and audited.

[16:36] Jonas Richter: Blocking metering sounds dangerous. Would that fail the request?

[16:40] Naomi Feldman: For some artifacts, yes we fail closed. For others, we can decouple and ensure no payload is exported cross-region, but still preserve request availability. The POC can validate your preference. For strict compliance tenants we typically prioritize “don’t violate residency” even if that means a request fails.

[17:02] Sven Adler: We’d rather fail than violate.

[17:05] Marianne Dupont: Same.

[17:06] Markus Klein: Cool. That aligns.

[17:10] (crosstalk)

[17:12] Lukas Meyer: Okay. Let’s nail the scope: One dedicated EU region, pinned region policy, one primary chat model, maybe one embeddings model, IP allowlisting, audit logs export samples, load test session, and a short security review pack.

[17:28] Aditi Rao: For models, can you share what you recommend? We’re currently on GPT-4 class for some tasks, but we can compromise.

[17:36] Markus Klein: We can propose a couple: a 70B open model for chat with good instruction following, plus maybe a smaller model for classification. For embeddings we can use a standard high-quality embedding model. We’ll put options in the follow-up.

[17:53] Sven Adler: Okay.

[17:55] Jonas Richter: Where do we see metrics? Is there a console?

[17:59] Markus Klein: Yes, Redwood Console. For dedicated you’ll see latency, tokens/sec, error codes. There’s also a residency violations view in the console in the newer build—still behind a flag, but we can enable in POC.

[18:16] Jonas Richter: Good.

[18:18] Marianne Dupont: And audit logs—do you have Splunk format?

[18:22] Naomi Feldman: We have sample payloads and field mappings for Splunk and Sentinel. The key fields are tenant/org id, decision, pinned/allowed region, request id, actor (API key), and reason.

[18:38] Sven Adler: That’s exactly what we need.

[18:41] Lukas Meyer: Great. Any blockers we haven’t discussed?

[18:45] Jonas Richter: I worry about “streaming” through gateways. Some providers buffer.

[18:50] Markus Klein: We do true streaming, chunked responses. In dedicated it’s straightforward. We can test it early.

[18:58] Aditi Rao: Also, retries: if request fails due to region mismatch, we don’t want SDK to retry in a different region.

[19:06] Markus Klein: Good catch. Our SDK can treat that error as non-retriable. The error code is explicit. That’s part of the beta work.

[19:15] Naomi Feldman: Residency violations are considered hard failures. Retrying won’t help unless you change endpoint/config.

[19:24] Sven Adler: Nice.

[19:26] Lukas Meyer: Okay, let’s do recap and next steps.

[19:29] Lukas Meyer: I’ll send a POC plan email by tomorrow: scope, timeline, and what you need to provide. Markus will send sizing recommendation by Friday after you share the traffic shape. Naomi will send audit event samples and the error code behavior write-up. You’ll send: traffic summary, IP ranges, and confirm models you want to test.

[19:55] Sven Adler: Works.

[19:56] Marianne Dupont: Yes.

[19:58] Jonas Richter: Yep.

[20:00] Aditi Rao: Okay.

[20:02] Lukas Meyer: Any last questions?

[20:05] Marianne Dupont: Just one: GA timeline for the residency enforcement.

[20:09] Naomi Feldman: We’re targeting GA after beta validation—roughly end of quarter. For your POC, we can document current behavior and what changes at GA (mostly defaults and UI polish).

[20:24] Marianne Dupont: Okay.

[20:25] Lukas Meyer: Great. Thanks everyone. We’ll follow up in email and set the technical deep dive.

[20:33] (Meeting continues with light scheduling / goodbyes; transcript ends early due to recording cutoff.)
